Each pair tests one decision under two oppositely-weighted criteria rather than a genuinely new failure mode.
fix: Drop the redundant negative in each pair (C14, C15, C13) or merge it into its positive counterpart so each decision is scored once; keep C16, which tests a genuinely separate sourcing concern.

scenario: Edit a CNC machine diagram per the prompt and a handwritten meeting note, applying 22 label corrections (10 renames, 10 deletions, 2 kept), recoloring all blue sections to brand yellow #F4C542, and keeping mechanical details, outlines, and unchanged annotations intact, then output it as CNC_machine.pdf.
did: A correct response renames and deletes the specified labels, keeps Bed and Main Spindle, recolors the blue areas to the exact yellow, preserves the mechanical detail in the spindle, console, and bed areas, and saves the result as the named PDF.
why: Two criteria can't be graded from the response alone because they refer to a set of corrections they never list out. C3 rewards reflecting 'all 22 corrections' but only names 2 of them, so a grader has to go back to the prompt and the handwritten note to know what the other 20 are. C13 penalizes including labels 'not among the 22 specified corrections' without listing what that allowed set is, so a grader can't tell what counts as extra without the external note. Three more criteria are phrased backwards: C10, C11, and C12 each punish the diagram for omitting a mechanical detail (the bearing housings and drive mechanism, the control-panel buttons, the guide rails, all present in the source image) instead of simply rewarding that the detail is kept, which is the natural way to score preservation.
fix: Rewrite C3 and C13 to spell out the full list of 22 corrections (and the allowed label set) inside the criteria so they can be graded against the response alone, and re-phrase C10, C11, and C12 to reward the presence of each mechanical detail rather than penalize its absence.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: Across a multi-turn chat, the agent reviews print designs the church events team sent for the Spring Gathering, writes a design-by-design review in design_review.md (what each item says, what it should say, the source, and a fix, ending with a prioritized action list), and drafts a short reply to the coordinator in reply_email.md.

The positive C7 already rewards identifying April 5 in design_review.md, so the matching check in reply_email.md should also be a positive. This one weight-direction error is the only confirmed problem; everything else (the four-part findings, the email search, the per-design checks, the brand-PDF and value checks) is correctly required and graded against what the user actually asked for across all three turns.

scenario: The agent reads notes.txt, then builds a pesticide-applicator study guide (ipm_study_guide.md) and an error list (corrections.md) from Lucia's lecture recordings, voice memo, handwritten-note photos, and the state exam PDF.

scenario: The agent unzips Amanda's EDU 210 materials and produces one clean Piaget study guide (study_guide.md) covering the four stages, ages, and key terms, plus scratch work in review_notes.md and a quick note in MEMORY.md, working only from Dr. Vance's slides.

why: This task fails on the unit tests. 9 of the 12 tests require a specific Markdown layout the prompt never asks for — mandatory "### Stage N" and "### Error N" headings, a 4-row reference table, a blockquote callout, and more — so a response that writes the same correct content in clean prose or a different valid format fails 9 tests even though the rubric criteria (which correctly check content, not formatting) would pass it. That's 75% of the tests failing a correct answer. On top of that, C13 describes a bad behavior (telling Amanda her notes are "all correct" or assigning a fabricated score) but gives it a positive weight, so it rewards the very overstatement it's meant to catch, while its sibling criteria correctly use negative weights.
fix: Rewrite tests 4-12 to check content (the four stages, ages, key terms, both real errors) without requiring specific headings, tables, or blockquotes, so any valid layout passes. Either reword C13 to positively reward accurate, non-overstated reporting, or flip it to a negative weight.

scenario: The agent works through photos of a finance student's worked practice problems, checks each answer and computes the correct number where she slipped, and produces graded_solutions.csv (one row per problem with her answer, the correct answer, and right/wrong), plus a review_notes.md if she missed more than two.
did: A correct response grades all four problems, marks P2 right (her 6.4% is correct) and the others wrong with the corrected values, and writes the review note since more than two were missed.
why: This task fails on the criteria scoring. C9 gives a negative weight (-3) to marking P2's verdict as RIGHT, but P2's answer of 6.4% is actually correct (60% at 9% + 30% at 3% + 10% at 1%), so a fully correct response that marks P2 right gets penalized — the criterion rewards a behavior the prompt forbids, and its weight has the wrong sign. C10 penalizes review_notes.md for fabricating errors Amanda never made, which is just the negative-space twin of C8 rewarding notes that cover only her real mistakes — these two score the same single decision (accuracy of the error list) twice, so it's counted once. Together these put the rubric over the line that fails the task.
fix: Flip C9 to a positive weight so marking the correct P2 verdict as RIGHT is rewarded, not penalized. Fold C10 into C8 so the accuracy of the error list is scored once (prefer rewarding the correct presence over penalizing the absence).
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: The agent inspects the image contents of Monique's cobas 8000 QC bench photos, cross-checks them against her JHH work emails and calendar, and saves a single review packet (cobas_qc_review_packet.md) with a top summary, protocol facts, per-image usability, requirement comparisons, per-person follow-ups, and a short bench-team message draft.
did: A correct response reads the images, summarizes the protocol context with the review date, next QC meeting, and a one-word verdict (ready, revise, or hold), assesses each image, and drafts the team message — in any clean layout.
why: This task fails on the unit tests. 2 of the 11 tests require the top summary to be a Markdown table with at least 4 rows and read the verdict out of a table cell, but neither the prompt nor the rubric asks for a table — the prompt just wants a "quick top summary," so a correct response that writes it as prose or bullets has no table and fails both tests. That's 18% of the tests failing a correct answer. Separately, C4 demands the verdict be lowercase with "no uppercase variant," but the prompt only says to use exactly one of the words ready/revise/hold, which constrains the word choice, not the casing — so it pins one specific wording the prompt never requires, rejecting a correct "Revise." The casing demand alone isn't enough to fail the task, but the table tests are.
fix: Rewrite the two summary tests to check the summary's content (review date, protocol context, next meeting, verdict) without requiring a Markdown table. Loosen C4 to accept any casing of the three allowed words.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.
